headline: Do six jams sell better than twenty-four?
title: When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: A supermarket tasting table alternated between six and twenty-four jams. The larger display attracted more shoppers, but a greater share of those who stopped at the smaller display went on to buy jam. A meta-analysis of choice-overload experiments found an average effect near zero and substantial variation across studies. This addresses the broader claim about choice set size. https://doi.org/10.1086/651235

headline: Are branded search ads getting credit for people who were going to buy anyway?
title: Consumer Heterogeneity and Paid Search Effectiveness: A Large-Scale Field Experiment
note: The researchers turned off selected eBay search ads and compared outcomes with controls. Brand-keyword ads produced no measurable short-term benefit in the experiment, while nonbrand effects varied by customer type.

headline: Can an expensive logo make strangers treat the same person differently?
title: Social Benefits of Luxury Brands as Costly Signals of Wealth and Status
note: The original studies reported more favorable responses when clothing displayed luxury labels. An extended replication recovered higher ratings of wealth and status but did not consistently recover the behavioral benefits. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0170216

headline: Does the decoy effect survive when shoppers see products instead of a table of numbers?
title: The Limits of Attraction
note: The authors tested decoys across several ways of presenting options and reported limited evidence with perceptual or qualitative attributes. The original authors responded that some procedures used decoys unlikely to work. https://doi.org/10.1509/jmr.14.0208

headline: Can elaborate targeting controls recover the lift that a randomized Facebook ad test measures?
title: A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook
note: Comparing observational methods with randomized estimates across Facebook campaigns, the authors found that detailed control variables often failed to recover the experimental effect.

headline: Buy an energy drink on sale, solve fewer puzzles?
title: Placebo Effects of Marketing Actions: Consumers May Get What They Pay For
note: Participants paid different prices for the same energy drink. The researchers reported that those who paid a discounted price solved fewer puzzles afterward than those who paid full price.

headline: See an Apple logo, find a new use for a brick?
title: Automatic Effects of Brand Exposure on Motivated Behavior: How Apple Makes You “Think Different”
note: After brief exposure to either the Apple or IBM logo, participants brainstormed uses for a brick. Judges rated the Apple group's ideas as more creative.

headline: When would you stop eating a bowl of soup that never empties?
title: Bottomless Bowls: Why Visual Cues of Portion Size May Influence Intake
note: Hidden tubing slowly refilled soup bowls while diners ate. Researchers measured how much soup people consumed from the secretly refilling bowls and from regular bowls.

headline: Can a supermarket playlist sell French wine one day and German wine the next?
title: In-store music affects product choice
note: Researchers alternated French and German music near a supermarket wine display and tracked sales. French wine outsold German wine when French music played. The ranking reversed when German music played.

headline: Would you bid more for the same basketball tickets if you paid by credit card?
title: Always Leave Home Without It: A Further Investigation of the Credit-Card Effect on Willingness to Pay
note: Participants in actual auctions submitted higher bids in credit-card conditions than under cash payment. A later meta-analysis estimated a small average cashless spending effect across different settings and measures. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jretai.2024.05.003

headline: Can the same 29% increase look bigger just because you change the units?
title: How to Make a 29% Increase Look Bigger: The Unit Effect in Option Comparisons
note: Consumers compared differences expressed in equivalent units. Changing the size of the displayed numbers altered how large participants judged the difference to be.

headline: Can an overfilled little cup of ice cream seem worth more than a larger serving when you see them one at a time?
title: Less Is Better: When Low-Value Options Are Valued More Highly than High-Value Options
note: Separate evaluations favored the overfilled smaller serving in the reported task. When the servings were evaluated together, the larger quantity became easier to compare directly.

headline: Can a decoy sometimes make its intended target less attractive?
title: More Evidence Challenging the Robustness and Usefulness of the Attraction Effect
note: The authors varied how shoppers encountered products and reported that the expected effect was often weak, absent or reversed with more naturalistic stimuli.

headline: Why would cutting both chocolate prices by the same amount make people switch brands?
title: Zero as a Special Price: The True Value of Free Products
note: The experiments varied chocolate prices while preserving the price gap. When the cheaper chocolate became free, its choice share rose more than under the positive-price comparisons.

headline: Does hiding the fee until checkout make people buy better seats?
title: Price Salience and Product Choice
note: In a randomized StubHub experiment, showing fees later increased purchases and shifted buyers toward higher-priced tickets compared with showing fees at the start.

headline: Why can experiments with millions of customers still have trouble estimating ad returns?
title: The Unfavorable Economics of Measuring the Returns to Advertising
note: The study examined large randomized ad experiments and explained how noisy sales and small average treatment effects can create wide uncertainty about return on investment.

headline: Does calling the same dish a salad instead of pasta change how much dieters eat?
title: The Impact of Product Name on Dieters’ and Nondieters’ Food Evaluations and Consumption
note: Experiments used alternative names for the same foods. Dieters' evaluations and consumption were more responsive to the labels in the reported tasks.

headline: Can a product placement be memorable for the very reason it hurts the brand?
title: Investigating the Effectiveness of Product Placements in Television Shows: The Role of Modality and Plot Connection Congruence on Brand Memory and Attitude
note: When placement modality and connection to the plot did not fit, memory could improve while brand attitudes became less favorable. The outcome depended on whether the study scored recall or evaluation.

headline: Can more information bring the decoy effect back when options are shown as pictures?
title: Beyond Numbers: An Ambiguity–Accessibility–Applicability Framework to Explain the Attraction Effect
note: A follow-up tested how ambiguity and access to comparison information shape decoy effects. Its results identify conditions under which the effect can occur with nonnumerical attributes.

headline: Can moving a logo higher on the box make the brand look more powerful?
title: Place the Logo High or Low? Using Conceptual Metaphors of Power in Packaging Design
note: The experiments varied vertical logo position and measured attitudes toward packaging for brands with different power associations. Results depended on the match between position and brand image.

headline: Will grocery shoppers buy less when the tax is printed on the shelf tag?
title: Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence
note: Posting tax-inclusive tags in a grocery store reduced sales of treated products compared with the study's comparison products. Prices at checkout did not change as a result of the label intervention.

headline: Does a big assortment help if shoppers already know what they want?
title: When More Is Less and Less Is More: The Role of Ideal Point Availability and Assortment in Consumer Choice
note: The experiments found that the effect of assortment size depended in part on whether people could specify their preferred combination of features. This tested a condition that can change the outcome of adding more options.

headline: When does $2.99 seem much cheaper than $3.00?
title: Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition
note: Experiments reported a left-digit effect when a small price change crossed a digit boundary. A later meta-analysis found generally small effects of just-below prices, with variation by outcome. https://doi.org/10.1002/jcpy.1353

headline: How much did television advertising actually sell across 288 brands?
title: TV Advertising Effectiveness and Profitability: Generalizable Results From 288 Brands
note: The researchers applied common procedures across brands and found many small, statistically imprecise or negative estimates. They assessed the sensitivity of estimated advertising elasticities to measurement and model choices.

headline: Is an IKEA box worth more once you've built it yourself?
title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love
note: Participants assembled IKEA boxes, folded origami or built Lego sets. The researchers reported that people who successfully completed the task valued their own creations more highly.

headline: Turn a product around in an ad. Does it become easier to sell?
title: The “Visual Depiction Effect” in Advertising: Facilitating Embodied Mental Simulation through Product Orientation
note: Researchers changed which way a product faced in an ad. They reported that people could more readily imagine using it and wanted to buy it more when it faced their dominant hand.

headline: Lean back in your chair, pick the middle option?
title: Consumer Behavior in “Equilibrium”: How Experiencing Physical Balance Increases Compromise Choice
note: Across six experiments, researchers studied physical balance and shopping decisions. One example involved leaning back in a chair while shopping online. They reported that experiencing balance made people more likely to choose products with middle-of-the-road features.

headline: Does important information make a storage device feel heavier?
title: Weighty data: importance information influences estimated weight of digital information storage devices
note: The authors tested whether descriptions of the importance of digital contents changed perceived weight of their storage media.

headline: Does it start feeling like yours before you've even paid?
title: The Effect of Mere Touch on Perceived Ownership
note: Researchers varied whether people could touch an object, then asked how much it felt like their own. People who had touched the object reported a stronger sense of ownership.

headline: Would you still buy it after another shopper had handled it?
title: Consumer Contamination: How Consumers React to Products Touched by Others
note: Researchers varied the signs that another shopper had touched a product, then asked people to evaluate products or choose among them. They reported lower ratings when the signs of prior contact were more apparent.

headline: Would you pick a brand that starts with letters from your own name?
title: Name Letter Branding: Valence Transfers When Product Specific Needs Are Active
note: Across five experiments, the researchers studied brand choices. They reported a preference for brands starting with letters from the shopper's name when the product met an immediate need.

headline: Can a red screen change what you're willing to pay?
title: The Effect of Red Background Color on Willingness-to-Pay: The Moderating Role of Selling Mechanism
note: The authors reported that red backgrounds increased bids in auctions but reduced offers in negotiations.

headline: Would you spend a crumpled bill sooner than a crisp one?
title: Money Isn’t Everything, but It Helps If It Doesn’t Look Used: How the Physical Appearance of Money Influences Spending
note: Researchers compared spending choices involving worn and crisp notes. They reported that people were more willing to spend worn bills and placed a premium on keeping crisp ones.

headline: Is one $20 bill harder to part with than twenty singles?
title: The Denomination Effect
note: Three field studies varied the denominations people received while keeping the total amount the same. People given one large bill were less likely to spend any of the money.

headline: Does a dress sell better when the price ends in 9?
title: Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments
note: Researchers varied prices for the same women's clothing across mail-order catalogs and tracked actual orders. In all three field experiments, demand was higher for prices ending in 9 dollars.

headline: Want diners to pick the healthier food? Put it on the left?
title: Healthy-Left, Unhealthy-Right: Can Displaying Healthy Items to the Left (versus Right) of Unhealthy Items Nudge Healthier Choices?
note: Participants chose between healthier and less healthy foods. The authors reported that the healthier option was chosen more often when it appeared on the left.

headline: Does a round logo make a product look more comfortable?
title: Does Your Company Have the Right Logo? How and Why Circular- and Angular-Logo Shapes Influence Brand Attribute Judgments
note: Participants rated products bearing differently shaped logos. The authors reported that round logos brought softness to mind and angular logos brought hardness to mind.

headline: Does warming up the customer make the product worth more?
title: The temperature premium: Warm temperatures increase product valuation
note: Five studies reported higher product valuations when consumers experienced warmer physical temperatures.

headline: Can a smell steer you toward a brand?
title: Olfactory priming on consumer categorization, recall, and choice
note: Experiments reported differences in recall and choice of objects or brands associated with scents diffused in the surroundings.

headline: Does writing down how much you spent change how much you spend next?
title: Effects of Payment Mechanism on Spending Behavior: The Role of Rehearsal and Immediacy of Payments
note: Experiments varied whether payment drew attention to the amount and how soon it reduced available funds. Subsequent spending decisions depended on the procedure.

headline: Does the payment method change how much junk food ends up in the cart?
title: How Credit Card Payments Increase Unhealthy Food Purchases: Visceral Regulation of Vices
note: The paper combined store records with experiments and reported a relationship between card payment and purchases classified as vice foods. The transaction analysis and the controlled tasks used different designs.

headline: Does paying for a ticket long ago make it easier to waste?
title: Payment Depreciation: The Behavioral Effects of Temporally Separating Payments from Consumption
note: In decision scenarios, separating the payment from later consumption reduced the weight placed on the prior cost. The result concerns the timing and framing used in the tasks.

headline: Do people judge the same specification differently when it is written in an unfamiliar unit?
title: Are All Units Created Equal? The Effect of Default Units on Product Evaluations
note: The study varied how product specifications were expressed and reported that familiarity with the standard unit can change evaluations, beyond the effect of number size.

headline: Does splitting a price into a base price and surcharge make the total seem lower?
title: Divide and Prosper: Consumers’ Reactions to Partitioned Prices
note: The experiments compared a single total with a price split into components. The split affected recalled total cost and demand in the studied tasks.

headline: Can an irrelevant number change the price a buyer offers more than the price a seller demands?
title: Anchoring Effects on Consumers' Willingness-to-Pay and Willingness-to-Accept
note: The authors compared anchors in buying and selling tasks. Effects depended on the task and whether the anchor related to the valuation the participant was making.

headline: Can the price of something unrelated change what you pay for the item you actually want?
title: Incidental Prices and Their Effect on Willingness to Pay
note: Field and laboratory experiments reported effects on willingness to pay after exposure to prices of unrelated products, even when those products supplied no direct information about the target.

headline: Can labeling identical candy pieces as different kinds make people tire of them more slowly?
title: Reducing Satiation: The Role of Categorization Level
note: The experiments made people attend to narrower or broader categories while consuming items. Narrower categorization slowed the decline in reported enjoyment in the studied tasks.

headline: Do people pick more flavors when they order all their future snacks at once?
title: The Effect of Purchase Quantity and Timing on Variety-Seeking Behavior
note: Participants selected more variety when choosing several future snacks together than when making the selections separately over time. The comparison held the number of consumption occasions fixed.

headline: Can an online display ad affect store sales even when the customer never clicks?
title: Online Ads and Offline Sales: Measuring the Effect of Retail Advertising via a Controlled Experiment on Yahoo!
note: A randomized Yahoo! campaign linked assignment to later retail purchases. The study attributed most of the measured sales increase to offline stores, with much of the increase coming from people who did not click the ads.

headline: Is an ad for the exact hotel you viewed sometimes worse than a generic ad?
title: When Does Retargeting Work? Information Specificity in Online Advertising
note: A randomized travel-site campaign compared generic advertisements with advertisements showing the specific hotel previously viewed. Relative effectiveness varied with browsing behavior used to infer how developed a preference was.

headline: Do personalized ads become less persuasive when people see how their data were collected?
title: Unraveling the Personalization Paradox: The Effect of Information Collection and Trust-Building Strategies on Online Advertisement Effectiveness
note: The studies compared overt and covert information collection and varied trust cues. The authors found that consumer reactions to targeting depended on how the collection was presented.

headline: Will shoppers respond differently when a store smells like the gender category of its clothes?
title: Gender-Congruent Ambient Scent Influences on Approach and Avoidance Behaviors in a Retail Store
note: In a retail field experiment, the authors compared scent cues they classified as masculine or feminine and reported interactions with the merchandise category.

headline: Can making a product description harder to process make the product feel more special?
title: Making Products Feel Special: When Metacognitive Difficulty Enhances Evaluation
note: The authors varied processing difficulty and found that it could improve evaluations under conditions where they expected difficulty to signal distinctiveness.

headline: Do extra boxes on a shelf make a brand easier to see without making it more attractive?
title: Does In-Store Marketing Work? Effects of the Number and Position of Shelf Facings on Brand Attention and Evaluation at the Point of Purchase
note: Shelf experiments measured visual attention separately from brand evaluation. Increasing facings or changing shelf position affected attention, and effects on evaluation depended on the design and brand.

headline: How many apparent sales from a free sample would have happened anyway?
title: The Effects of Free Sample Promotions on Incremental Brand Sales
note: The study separated expansion, accelerated purchasing, and purchases that sampling substituted for. Its analysis illustrated why counts of purchases following samples can differ from estimated incremental sales.

headline: Does wanting to look high-status make people choose green products in public?
title: Going Green to Be Seen: Status, Reputation, and Conspicuous Conservation
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Status motives increased preference for green products in public or higher-cost scenarios in the reported experiments. The studies measured choices in the scenarios presented.

headline: Why would some wealthy shoppers pay more to make a luxury logo harder to see?
title: Signaling Status with Luxury Goods: The Role of Brand Prominence
note: The authors combined brand and product observations with experiments and modeled how preferences for prominent logos varied with wealth and status motives.

headline: Can cold tea help you regulate the feeling of regret?
title: The warmth of our regrets: Managing regret through physiological regulation and consumption
note: The researchers used regret manipulations and measured preferences for hot and cold drinks.

headline: Does loud noise make shoppers choose visually quiet products?
title: Crossmodal compensation: Sensory discomfort affects consumer preferences across modalities
note: The experiments investigate choices in one sensory modality after discomfort in another.

headline: Does drinking something cold make you want more social products?
title: Embodied cognition and social consumption: Self-regulating temperature through social products and behaviors
note: The experiments examined associations between physical warmth and socially oriented consumption.

headline: Can the color red make you use less skin cream as well as eat less?
title: The effect of the color red on consuming food does not depend on achromatic (Michelson) contrast and extends to rubbing cream on the skin
note: Researchers compared amounts of food sampled and cream used under different color conditions and reported lower consumption with red.

headline: Does imagining a smell make a product feel closer?
title: So Close I Can Almost Sense It: The Interplay between Sensory Imagery and Psychological Distance
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can the way your tongue moves make you prefer a brand name?
title: Articulation Patterns in Names: A Hidden Route to Consumer Preference
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: The authors examined whether the direction of articulatory movements when pronouncing invented names affects consumers' preferences.

headline: Can a warm room make investors and consumers follow the crowd?
title: Warmth and conformity: The effects of ambient temperature on product preferences and financial decisions
note: The authors related temperature to conformity in shopping, price forecasts and betting.

headline: Does chocolate cake taste worse in front of a mirror?
title: Healthy Reflections: The Influence of Mirror-Induced Self-Awareness on Taste Perceptions
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: Students chose chocolate cake or fruit salad and tasted it in a room with or without a mirror. Among those who chose the cake, diners in front of a mirror gave it lower taste ratings.

headline: Can the consonants in a drug name make it sound more powerful?
title: A sound brand name: The role of voiced consonants in pharmaceutical branding
note: The authors investigated whether voiced consonants in invented medicine names affect consumers' expectations of potency and duration of action.

headline: Can a soundtrack change the taste of wine?
title: The effect of background music on the taste of wine
note: Participants tasted wine with different background music. The authors reported that their taste descriptions corresponded to characteristics of the music.

headline: Can a heavier package make a drink taste different?
title: Touch-flavor transference: Assessing the effect of packaging weight on gustatory evaluations, desire for food and beverages, and willingness to pay
note: The authors investigated whether package weight changed taste evaluations and valuation of the contents.

headline: Can the weight or color of a spoon change the taste of food?
title: The taste of cutlery: how the taste of food is affected by the weight, size, shape, and colour of the cutlery used to eat it
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does the shape and color of a plate change the taste of dinner?
title: Is it the plate or is it the food? Assessing the influence of the color (black or white) and shape of the plate on the perception of the food placed on it
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does a brand name sound like a round cookie?
title: What’s in a name? The effects of sound symbolism and package shape on consumer responses to food products
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can a simple fragrance make shoppers spend more?
title: The Power of Simplicity: Processing Fluency and the Effects of Olfactory Cues on Retail Sales
note: The researchers compared simpler and more complex ambient fragrances and spending behavior.

headline: Do people buy lucky products when they feel out of control?
title: Conditioned Superstition: Desire for Control and Consumer Brand Preferences
note: Five experiments reported stronger preferences for products previously paired with positive outcomes among people with a combination of high desire for control and low perceived control.
